opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's become one of the more useful tools in my workflow, though in a specific way. The best way I'd describe it is that it's like having a really fast, really diligent first-year grad student or research associate who will go off and read a couple hundred papers and come back with a structured synthesis in twenty minutes. That's an enormous unlock, because so much of science is just figuring out the state of the field before you can even ask a good question.

Where it shines for me is breadth. Say I want to understand everything that's been tried for delivering gene editors to a particular tissue, or what's known about some obscure protein family. It'll pull together the landscape, the key papers, the competing hypotheses, and it'll do it in a way that would've taken a person days. Even when it's not perfect, it gets me to the frontier of a topic much faster, and then I can spend my own time on the parts that actually require judgment.

Where I'm more careful is depth and taste. It's still not great at knowing which papers to trust. In biology, a lot of the literature doesn't replicate, and an expert carries a mental model of which labs are rigorous, which results everyone quietly knows are shaky, and which methods have hidden artifacts. The model tends to weight things more evenly than a seasoned scientist would. So I treat its output as a map, not the territory. I'll check the citations, go to the primary data, and sanity-check the claims that matter.

The other thing I'd say is that the bar is shifting. A year or two ago the question was "does this hallucinate?" Now the question is more "does this have scientific judgment?" Can it tell me what the interesting unanswered question is, not just summarize what's been done? That's the next frontier, and it's where I'm most excited, because if these systems can start proposing good hypotheses and designing experiments, that starts to change how we actually do biology, not just how we read about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes Deep Research’s practical role in Hsu’s workflow, but it does not distinguish that impact from interest or entertainment he derives from other AI applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's become one of the tools I reach for most. I think the way to describe it is that it's not replacing the thinking, it's replacing the grunt work that precedes the thinking. In biology, so much of what we do is literature synthesis. Before you design an experiment, you need to know what's been tried, what the failure modes were, which labs have worked on the problem, what the reagents are. That used to be a grad student spending a week reading. Now I can kick off a query in the morning and have a pretty reasonable first-pass review back by the time I'm out of my first meeting.

Where it's genuinely good is breadth. It'll surface papers from adjacent fields that I wouldn't have thought to look for, because I don't know the vocabulary that a structural biologist or a materials scientist uses for the same underlying phenomenon. That cross-pollination is real and it's valuable.

Where I'm more cautious is depth and judgment. It'll confidently tell you a result is established when it's actually one paper from 2009 that nobody's replicated. It doesn't have a good sense of which labs are reliable, which findings the field quietly doesn't believe anymore. That's tacit knowledge, and it's not in the text, so the model can't get it from reading. So I treat the output as a very well-read undergrad's report. Great starting point, but you'd never cite it without checking.

The other thing I'd say is that it's changed how I allocate my own attention. I spend less time collecting and more time deciding. And for a scientist, that's exactly the trade you want. The bottleneck in research was never reading papers. It was knowing which question to ask next. If these tools compress the front end, we get to spend more time on the part that actually matters.

r001.rationale: The response describes Deep Research changing Hsu’s work practices, including literature review and attention allocation, but does not distinguish that impact from interest or entertainment he gets from other AI applications.

astra-6.text: For me, the test is whether it helps me get to a useful scientific question faster. Can it pull together a literature I don’t know well, surface connections I might have missed, and give me sources I can actually check? That’s where something like Deep Research could be valuable. But a polished report isn’t necessarily a correct report. I’d still want to read the key papers and check whether the evidence supports the conclusions. The real measure is whether it improves the next experiment or decision, not just whether it saves me some reading.

r001.rationale: The response describes how Deep Research might support scientific work, but it does not distinguish that impact from interest or entertainment Patrick gets from other AI applications.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the test is whether it helps me get to a useful answer faster—and whether I can verify that answer. In research, a polished summary isn’t enough. I want to follow the citations, understand what the evidence supports, and see where there’s uncertainty. If it helps me orient to a question and identify what I should read closely, that’s useful. I’d still want to check the underlying work before building on it.
